sysd-reliab-146.title: Chroot: changing what a program thinks the root is
sysd-reliab-146.text: A program can be fooled about where the file system begins. Chroot, a Unix command and system call, changes the apparent root directory for a process. In this chroot jail a program cannot name, and normally cannot reach, files outside the tree. Engineers use it to build and test software against only its expected dependencies, and to run legacy software whose libraries would clash with the host's. It is a weak jail: a privileged program can often chroot again to break out, and it limits no I/O, bandwidth, disk space or CPU time. The isolation of {{ref:sysd-reliab-063}} can be seen as an advanced form of it.

sysd-reliab-050.title: Kubernetes: a cluster that steers itself toward the state you declare
sysd-reliab-050.text:
A cluster of machines is a lot to keep in order by hand. Kubernetes, also known as K8s, is an open-source system that does it for you: it automates deploying, scaling and managing software. It assembles computers, virtual or bare metal, into a cluster (see {{ref:sysd-scale-075}}) that runs workloads packaged in {{ref:sysd-reliab-063}}. The software has two halves, a control plane and the nodes on which applications run.

Everything speaks one language. Kubernetes defines compute and storage as objects that can be managed as such. Its internal components, its extensions and the workloads on it all rely on the Kubernetes API. Its building blocks, called primitives, deploy, maintain and scale applications based on CPU, memory or custom metrics.

Kubernetes is not mere orchestration, which executes a defined workflow of first A, then B, then C. It is a set of independent, composable control processes that continuously drive the current state toward the desired state. Its design is greatly influenced by Google's internal system Borg.

In production the control plane usually runs across multiple computers and a cluster runs multiple nodes, which gives fault tolerance and high availability. Kubernetes is commonly used to host microservice-based systems, because it and its ecosystem of tools provide the capabilities those architectures need.

sysd-reliab-063.title: Containers: an application and everything it needs, isolated
sysd-reliab-063.text:
The promise of a container is that an application runs the same everywhere. A container is an isolated user-space instance that the operating system kernel allows alongside others, packaging an application with its dependencies. Programs inside can see only the container's contents and the devices assigned to it, and each container gets a subset of the computer's resources. The package holds the code and all its dependencies, such as specific runtime and library versions. The application therefore runs quickly and reliably from one computing environment to another. That decoupling lets container-based applications be deployed easily and consistently, and gives developers and operations teams a clear separation of responsibility between application logic and deployment.

Containers cost less than full virtualization. Their programs use the operating system's normal system call interface, so nothing is emulated and no intermediate machine layer sits in between. They are lightweight and use just the resources they need. Linux containers rely on Linux namespaces and {{ref:sysd-reliab-145}}, and the kernel often adds resource management so that one container's activity has limited impact on others.

The trade-off is flexibility. A container cannot host a guest operating system different from the host's, or a different guest kernel. On Linux, other distributions are fine, but Windows cannot be hosted. Typical uses are securely allocating finite hardware resources among many mutually distrusting users, and consolidating server hardware by moving services from separate hosts into containers on one server.

sysd-reliab-145.title: Cgroups: the kernel's budget for a group of processes
sysd-reliab-145.text: How does Linux stop one runaway process from eating the whole machine? Cgroups, short for control groups, is a Linux kernel feature that limits, accounts for and isolates the resource usage of a collection of processes. The resources include CPU, memory and disk I/O. A control group is a set of processes bound by the same criteria and tied to a set of limits. Groups are hierarchical, each inheriting limits from its parent. A group can be capped at a memory limit (including file system cache), I/O bandwidth, CPU quota, CPU set or open files. Some groups can get a larger share of CPU or disk I/O. Cgroups also measure usage, for billing for example. Cgroup v2 has a single process hierarchy and works on processes rather than threads, whereas v1 allowed multiple hierarchies; the first kernel supporting v2 was Linux 4.5. LXC, systemd and Kubernetes all use cgroups. Since Linux 4.19, the out-of-memory killer can kill a whole cgroup as a single unit to keep the workload intact.

sysd-reliab-064.title: Namespaces and cgroups: what a process sees and what it may use
sysd-reliab-064.text: Two kernel features let a process believe it owns a machine while keeping it from taking more than its share. Namespaces control what a process can see, and cgroups control how much of the system's resources it can use. Together they underpin Kubernetes, LXC and Podman. A namespace partitions kernel resources, so one set of processes sees one set of resources and another set sees a different one. Each gets the illusion of being the sole user of the system. As of Linux 5.6 there are eight kinds: mount, process ID, network, inter-process communication, UTS, user, cgroup and time. In a PID namespace the first process is PID 1, and its exit makes the kernel kill all others in that namespace. A network namespace has its own IP addresses, routing table and firewall rules. User namespaces map IDs between container and host, so a process can be root inside the container yet an unprivileged ID on the host.

sysd-reliab-227.title: Pod lifecycle: from Pending to Succeeded or Failed
sysd-reliab-227.text:
A Pod is disposable by design, and its lifecycle shows how. A Pod, the unit Kubernetes runs on a node, is created with a unique UID. It is scheduled to a node only once and stays there until it terminates or is deleted.

Its phase is a high-level summary, not a state machine. A Pod starts in Pending, which means it is accepted but its containers are not yet set up: it may be waiting to be scheduled or downloading images. It moves to Running once it is bound to a node and at least one primary container starts. It ends in Succeeded or Failed. Succeeded means all containers terminated in success and will not be restarted. Failed means all terminated and at least one failed, by a non-zero exit or a system kill. Unknown means the state could not be obtained, typically a node communication error.

Each container is Waiting, Running or Terminated, and a preStop hook runs before it terminates. The kubelet also records conditions, such as Initialized, ContainersReady and Ready. Ready means the Pod can serve requests and joins the load balancing pools of all matching Services. Readiness gates add custom conditions: the Pod is Ready only when its containers are ready and every gate is True.

The kubelet may restart a failed container, but a Pod that fails unrecoverably, sits on a failed node or is evicted is deleted. A Pod is never rescheduled. A near-identical replacement with a new UID takes over, maybe on another node, and anything tied to the old Pod's lifetime, such as a volume, is recreated.

sysd-reliab-161.title: Container probes: how Kubernetes decides a container is healthy
sysd-reliab-161.text: A container can be running and still be of no use: it may be deadlocked, or still warming its caches. Kubernetes finds out with probes, periodic checks (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-122}}) that the kubelet runs on a container, either by running code inside it or by making a network request. An exec probe treats exit code 0 as healthy. A TCP probe is healthy only if a connection to the port opens. An HTTP probe counts any status from 200 up to but not including 400 as success. A gRPC probe uses the gRPC Health Checking Protocol. Liveness probes decide when to restart a container, for example one that is deadlocked. Readiness probes decide when it can accept traffic, covering slow startup work such as warming caches. A startup probe runs only at startup, and until it succeeds no liveness or readiness probes run. For a slow-starting application, give it a failureThreshold times periodSeconds long enough for the worst-case startup, such as 30 * 10 = 300s.

sysd-reliab-045.title: Docker: containers that share one kernel
sysd-reliab-045.text: Every container on a Docker host shares one operating system kernel. That is why a server can run several at once and use fewer resources than machines that each boot their own system. Docker is a platform that packages software into containers using operating system-level virtualization. The containers are isolated from one another, bundle their own software, libraries and configuration files, and can communicate through well-defined channels. On Linux, Docker uses kernel isolation features such as cgroups and namespaces, plus a union-capable file system such as OverlayFS. Namespaces mostly isolate an application's view of its environment, including process trees, network, user IDs and mounted file systems, while cgroups limit memory and CPU. The Docker daemon, dockerd, is a persistent process that manages containers and listens for Docker Engine API requests, and the docker command-line client lets users talk to it. On macOS, Docker runs its containers inside a Linux guest system (see {{ref:sysd-reliab-065}}).

sysd-reliab-046.title: Container images and registries: how an application is shipped
sysd-reliab-046.text: A container starts from an image. A Docker image is a read-only template used to build containers, and images are how applications are stored and shipped. A Dockerfile, a text file, commonly specifies the Linux distribution of an image, the installation commands for the language runtime and the application source code. Images live in a registry, a repository that stores and serves them. Clients connect to it to download, or pull, images for use, and to upload, or push, images they have built. Docker Hub is the default registry where Docker looks for images, and it is a public registry that anyone can use. Registries can also create notifications based on events.

sysd-reliab-148.title: Container orchestration: replacing what fails, without downtime
sysd-reliab-148.text: In production, the containers running applications must be managed so that nothing goes down. Container orchestration automates that: it deploys, scales and manages containers so that one that fails is replaced by another without downtime. Kubernetes does this in several ways. It exposes a container by DNS name or IP address and load balances traffic when it is high. With automated rollouts and rollbacks, you describe the desired state and Kubernetes changes the actual state to match at a controlled rate. With automatic bin packing, you say how much CPU and memory each container needs and it fits them onto your nodes to make the best use of resources. Self-healing restarts and replaces failed containers, kills those that fail a user-defined health check, and does not advertise them to clients until they are ready to serve. Kubernetes is not an all-inclusive platform as a service, though: it works at the container level, does not build applications and has no built-in databases or message buses.

sysd-reliab-049.title: Container runtime: the software that starts and stops containers
sysd-reliab-049.text: Something has to actually start a container. That is the container runtime, the software responsible for the lifecycle of containers, including launching, reconciling and killing them. Every Kubernetes node must run one, and the kubelet, the agent on each node, talks to it through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI). The CRI decouples maintaining core Kubernetes from any one runtime. containerd and CRI-O are widely used CRI-compliant runtimes. Kubernetes was originally tightly coupled to Docker and dropped official Docker support as a runtime with v1.24 in May 2022. Docker Engine itself has been built on containerd and runc since version 1.11.

sysd-reliab-054.title: Kubernetes nodes: the machines that run the pods
sysd-reliab-054.text: Every few seconds, each node in a Kubernetes cluster reports its status to the API server in a heartbeat message. A node, also called a worker or minion, is a machine where containers are deployed. Every cluster has at least one, and it hosts the pods that make up the application workload. It runs a container runtime plus components that connect its containers to the network. The kubelet is an agent on each node that makes sure its pods' containers are running and healthy, starting, stopping and maintaining them as the control plane directs. When the control plane detects a node failure, a higher-level controller is expected to launch the pods on another healthy node. On each node, kube-proxy acts as a network proxy and load balancer, routing traffic to the appropriate container by the IP and port of the incoming request.

sysd-reliab-055.title: Kubernetes pods: the smallest thing Kubernetes runs
sysd-reliab-055.text: The smallest unit Kubernetes administers is not a container. It is a pod, the basic deployable unit, made of one or more containers co-located on the same node. In the most common case each pod has a single container. Each pod has a unique IP address within the cluster, shared by every container inside it, so applications can use ports without the risk of conflict. Containers in a pod reach each other on localhost, while containers in different pods have distinct IP addresses and talk over IP networking. A pod can also declare shared storage volumes, which let its data survive a container restart. Pods are ephemeral and disposable, so they are rarely created directly. A workload resource such as a Deployment creates them, replicates them for scale and replaces them when a node fails.

sysd-reliab-228.title: Pod restart policy: when a container that exits comes back
sysd-reliab-228.text: When a container exits, should Kubernetes start it again? The restartPolicy in a Pod spec answers that: Always, OnFailure or Never, with Always the default. Always restarts a container after any termination, OnFailure only if it exits with an error (a non-zero exit status), and Never not at all. Individual containers can override the Pod's policy with their own restartPolicy and ordered restartPolicyRules that compare the exit code with listed values; the first match applies. Sidecar containers ignore the Pod-level policy, since a sidecar is an init container whose own restartPolicy is Always. The RestartAllContainers action restarts the whole Pod in place. Containers stop without honoring the grace period or preStop hooks, init containers re-run, and the Pod keeps its UID, IP address and volumes. That suits workloads where rescheduling is costly, such as batch jobs or AI/ML training. The Kubernetes project advises designing for unannounced restarts either way.

sysd-reliab-229.title: CrashLoopBackOff: a container that keeps failing and waiting
sysd-reliab-229.text: The first time a container crashes, Kubernetes restarts it immediately. After repeated crashes it waits, using an exponential backoff (see {{ref:sysd-reliab-079}}), so a faulty container cannot swamp the system with failed starts. That cycle of failing, restarting and waiting is CrashLoopBackOff. Delays start at 10s and double each time up to a default cap of 300s, and running successfully for a duration such as 10 minutes resets them. Typical causes are application errors, bad configuration such as wrong environment variables or missing files, too little memory or CPU, and slow-starting applications failing health checks. Investigate with kubectl logs and kubectl describe pod.

sysd-reliab-230.title: Graceful pod termination: TERM first, KILL only after the grace period
sysd-reliab-230.text: A deleted Pod is not killed at once. Pods are processes, so they should terminate gracefully rather than be stopped abruptly with a KILL signal. When you request deletion, the cluster records the intended grace period. The kubelet then has the container runtime send a TERM signal to each container's main process so it can clean up. After the grace period, KILL goes to any remaining processes and the Pod is deleted from the API server. A preStop hook runs before a container enters the Terminated state, whereas an in-place Pod restart skips the grace period and preStop hooks.

sysd-reliab-061.title: Container persistent storage: data that outlives a container
sysd-reliab-061.text: In Kubernetes, a container's filesystem is wiped when the container restarts, which is limiting for anything but trivial applications. Data that must outlive a container needs a volume. A volume provides persistent storage and shared disk space for the containers in a pod, and the same volume can be mounted at different points by different containers. A Docker volume likewise lets data persist independently, remaining after a container is deleted or re-created. Kubernetes was historically suited only to stateless services (see {{ref:sysd-scale-138}}), but databases need persistence. The Container Storage Interface separated the code for external storage systems from the core Kubernetes code base.

sysd-reliab-159.title: Sidecar and init containers: helpers that share a Pod
sysd-reliab-159.text: Most Pods hold one container, but a Pod can hold several that cooperate. These containers are co-located, co-scheduled and share resources, and Kubernetes manages the Pod rather than the container. In a typical multi-container Pod, one container serves files from a shared volume to the public while a separate sidecar container refreshes those files from a remote source. Sidecar containers provide auxiliary services to the main application, such as a service mesh. Init containers by default run to completion before the application containers start. An init container with restartPolicy Always is a sidecar: it starts before the application and runs until the Pod shuts down.

sysd-reliab-060.title: Labels and selectors: how Kubernetes finds the right objects
sysd-reliab-060.text: Kubernetes tags its objects, and everything else finds them by tag. Labels are keys that clients attach to any API object, such as pods and nodes, and label selectors are queries that resolve to the matching objects. A service's label selector chooses the pod instances that its router or load balancer sends traffic to. Changing pod labels or a service's selector therefore controls which pods receive traffic, which supports deployment patterns such as {{ref:sysd-reliab-039}} or A/B testing. This dynamic control over which resources implement a service gives the infrastructure loose coupling.

sysd-reliab-058.title: Kubernetes services: one stable address for a changing set of pods
sysd-reliab-058.text: Pods are ephemeral, and the set of healthy ones changes from moment to moment, so a frontend cannot keep track of backend IP addresses. A Kubernetes service solves this. It is a set of pods that work together, such as one tier of a multi-tier application, and it gives that group one stable endpoint. A label selector defines which pods belong to it. Service discovery gives the service a stable IP address and DNS name. It load balances traffic round-robin across the matching pods, even as failures move pods from machine to machine. Kubernetes offers two modes of service discovery: environment variables or Kubernetes DNS. On each node, kube-proxy forwards requests to the correct containers. By default a service is exposed inside the cluster, for example back-end pods balancing requests from front-end pods, but it can also be exposed outside it.

sysd-reliab-151.title: Kubernetes Service types: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer and ExternalName
sysd-reliab-151.text:
Not every service should be reachable from everywhere, so Kubernetes lets you choose how each one is exposed. The type field is nested functionality, each level adding to the previous one, and several types build on ClusterIP as a foundation.

ClusterIP, the default, exposes the Service on a cluster-internal IP, so it is reachable only from within the cluster. A Gateway can expose it to the public internet, and so can the object described in {{ref:sysd-reliab-152}}. NodePort exposes the Service on each node's IP at a static port. The control plane allocates it from a range, by default 30000-32767, and every node proxies that same port into the Service.

LoadBalancer exposes the Service externally through a load balancer. Kubernetes offers no load balancing component itself, so you provide one or integrate with a cloud provider. A LoadBalancer Service typically starts as a NodePort Service, and the cloud-controller-manager then configures the external load balancer to forward traffic to that node port.

ExternalName maps the Service to a DNS name by returning a CNAME record for the external hostname, with no proxying of any kind. A headless Service sets the cluster IP to None, so no cluster IP is allocated and kube-proxy ignores it. DNS returns individual Pod IPs instead, so a client can connect to whichever Pod it prefers.

sysd-reliab-152.title: Kubernetes Ingress: HTTP routes into the cluster
sysd-reliab-152.text: Write an Ingress and nothing happens until a controller picks it up. An Ingress is a Kubernetes API object that exposes HTTP and HTTPS routes from outside the cluster to services inside it, using rules defined on the Ingress resource. An Ingress controller fulfils it, usually with a load balancer. It can give Services externally reachable URLs, load balance traffic, terminate SSL/TLS and offer name-based virtual hosting. Each rule has an optional host and a list of paths, each with a backend naming a Service and port. Both host and path must match before traffic is sent there. A fanout setup routes traffic from a single IP address to more than one Service based on the requested URI. That keeps the number of load balancers to a minimum. TLS ends at the ingress point, so traffic onward to Services and Pods is plaintext. An Ingress does not expose arbitrary ports or protocols; anything other than HTTP and HTTPS is usually exposed with a Service of type NodePort or LoadBalancer.

sysd-reliab-153.title: Ingress path and host matching: which backend gets the request
sysd-reliab-153.text: Which Service should answer a request for /foo/bar/baz? Ingress rules decide by matching the request's host and URL path. Every path needs a pathType, Exact, Prefix or ImplementationSpecific, or it fails validation. Exact matches the URL path exactly and case-sensitively, while Prefix matches element by element on the path split by slashes, so Prefix /foo/bar matches /foo/bar/baz but not /foo/barbaz. When several paths match, the longest wins, and between equal matches an Exact path beats a Prefix path. A host can be exact, such as foo.bar.com, or a wildcard such as *.foo.com, which covers a single DNS label. Anything unmatched goes to the default backend.

openers.containers-orchestration-and-deployment: A container packages an application with its dependencies so that it runs the same in any environment, and much of this chapter grows from that idea. First come the Linux kernel features that isolate containers, from chroot to namespaces and cgroups, which control what a process can see and how much of the system it can use. Next come Docker, with its images and registries, and Kubernetes, which orchestrates containers so that one that goes down is replaced by another without downtime. Along the way you will meet nodes, Pods and the probes the kubelet runs to learn whether a container is healthy.
